summary: Año Nuevo Light Station: a steam fog signal from 1872 and a light from 1890 on a rocky island off San Mateo County, deactivated in 1948 and now closed.

lens.note: Fourth-order light on the tank from 1911; the Fresnel lens moved into the 1914 skeleton tower (LighthouseFriends)

structures.note: Built beside the water tank; cut down by the state in 1976 (LighthouseFriends). USLHS gives 1890 and wood for the tower.
15,000-gallon tank; lantern room placed on top in 1911

access.note: Island owned by California State Parks; grounds and dwelling closed (LighthouseFriends). The point is reached by a 1.7-mile hike from the state park; on the island, guided walks only from December to March, to the point.

events.note: Twelve-inch steam whistle first sounded 29 May 1872
Fog station built on the island (SF Call, 1897)
Fog signal changed from a 15-second blast each minute to a 10-second blast and 55 seconds of silence (LighthouseFriends; the 1897 Call still describes 15 seconds)
Keeper Henry W. Colburn, assistant Bernard A. Ashley and two visitors (Clayton and Frank Pratt) drowned in a boat crossing to the mainland
Lens lantern on a post on the seaward side of the fog signal placed in operation 12 February 1890
Small frame structure with plate-glass panes built around the lens lantern; tramway rebuilt; storehouse built at the landing
Nine-room, two-story addition to the keepers' dwelling
Lantern room placed atop the water tank to display a fourth-order light
Listed among lights changed from fixed to flashing or occulting
Square skeleton tower built beside the water tank; Fresnel lens transferred into it (USLHS gives 1890 and wood for the tower)
Commissioner's report: keepers' dwellings still needed at a number of stations, including Ano Nuevo Island
Earthquake, 22 October 1926, 4:40 a.m.: lamp shaken into the lens and prisms shaken out; second shock at 5:45 a.m. tore the lens loose

Heavy seas in the storms of December and January (the Bulletin is of 1932; the passage does not name the winter): landing wharf, bulkheads, storehouse, fog-signal foundations, water tank and oil house damaged
Head keeper Kreth reported killer whales attacking a sperm whale near the station
Station deactivated; replaced by a whistle buoy about 1,600 yards south of the island
Island at auction; State of California acquired it in April 1958 for $51,094
State cut down the steel tower, likely to collapse; the toppled tower remains on the island

notes_for_editor: KEEPERS: the 112 roster lines are the USLHS archive's own stints, generated from roster.py --json; each carries the archive's person slug. USCG lines (4) have no stated position. Hugh Tighe's span is printed 'at least 1921-1923'. Roles are roster.py's normalisation. The roster is NARA keeper registers via the Kraig Anderson inventory; confirm any name in a primary record before naming it in print. CITATIONS: fiscal-year labels for the Light-House Board entries come from corpus.py page (report-year labels from the volume's boundaries); scan pages were read in the local OCR text, printed page numbers were not confirmed, so cite scan pages. The fog-whistle hours are the Board's own table lines for 'Ano Nuevo Island'; the 1899 coal figure is garbled in the OCR and is not used. UNVERIFIED LIGHTHOUSEFRIENDS DETAIL: the 1883 drowning, the wives' signal, Jip the dog, the 1916 sea lions, the 1939 killer whales, the 1926 quake details and the 1958 auction come from LighthouseFriends alone, which cites the 1897 SF Call, a 1916 Evening Telegram and a 2005 Bischoff article. The 1902 Board quotation ('barely sufficient for one') is LighthouseFriends quoting a 1902 report that is not in our corpus. CONFLICTS LEFT OPEN: (a) first light: the record's first_lit 1872 is the fog station; LighthouseFriends dates the first light to 12 Feb 1890 (correction proposed). (b) Tower: USLHS gives 1890 and wood; LighthouseFriends describes a steel skeleton tower built in 1914 and cut down in 1976; the record's 'tower, wood, built 1890' follows USLHS. Rowlett's 'Tower 3, 1914' was not read. (c) Fog-signal characteristic: LighthouseFriends says 1881 changed to 10 s blasts; the 1897 SF Call still says 15 s each minute. The 1897 SF Call says 'Eight of the fog-signal keepers have been drowned'; no other source here gives that count, so it is not repeated as fact. The 1927 Bulletin keeper's letter is not signed in the OCR, and the keeper on duty in October 1926 (Becker to 1926, Chambers from 1926 on the roster) is not named. The 1932 Bulletin passage says 'December and January' without a year. NOT JOINED: LighthouseFriends names John Ryan, first assistant at Pigeon Point in 1883, sent to take charge here; the roster's John C. Ryan (1883-1886) may be the same man, but no source connects them, so no other_stations entry is made. NOT PLACED: the Carrier Pigeon (1853), Sir John Franklin (1865) and Coya (1866), named by LighthouseFriends with no location. NEWSPAPERS: a Chronicling America search for the 1883 drowning in California papers found nothing; the 1880-1900 search found the 1897 SF Call article used here. COORDINATES: the record uses OSM (37.10784, -122.335689); USLHS gives 37.11222, -122.33083; LighthouseFriends gives 37.1084, -122.33676. Not proposed for change. Chronicling America and loc.gov were read only through newspapers.py. FACT-CHECK 2026-10-28: story corrected on the fact-check pass (1916 sea-lion complaint moved out of the Kreth paragraph; tower date and material conflict stated; 1932 storehouse damage restated; 1897 Call date clarified; units added).
